entities.name: Abuja National Mosque
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Nigerian National Mosque (Abuja National Mosque) in Abuja, Nigeria, inaugurated in 1984 — with its distinctive four minarets and golden dome visible from across the new capital city — was one of the first major structures built in Nigeria's planned federal capital Abuja, intended to serve Nigeria's approximately 100 million Muslims (roughly half the country's population, making it Africa's largest Muslim community by absolute numbers) and to symbolize the equal status of Islam and Christianity in Nigeria's secular federal republic.

Abuja itself was a planned capital designed from scratch and built in the 1980s to replace Lagos as Nigeria's capital, chosen for its central location that was intended to reduce ethnic and regional tensions in Africa's most populous country. The National Mosque and the nearby Nigerian National Christian Centre were built simultaneously and placed close together as physical symbols of Nigeria's constitutional commitment to religious equality — a deliberate architectural and political statement in a country where religious tensions (particularly between the predominantly Muslim north and predominantly Christian south) have periodically erupted into violence.

The mosque's architectural design draws on North African and Middle Eastern mosque traditions adapted to African context, with Saudi Arabian financial support for its construction reflecting Gulf states' investment in West African Islamic infrastructure. The mosque serves as the site of national Islamic prayers on Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha, attended by Nigeria's head of state, and functions as a symbol of the federal government's formal recognition of Islam's place in Nigerian public life.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Abuja National Mosque — serving Africa's largest Muslim community, built as a deliberate symbol of Nigerian religious equality alongside the National Christian Centre, and a Gulf-funded assertion of Islamic presence in Africa's most populous country — is a key monument in West African Islamic and political history.
